Course Description 
The Marketing and Management course is designed to equip students with the foundational skills 
and knowledge necessary to excel in the dynamic fields of marketing and management. This 
comprehensive course offers a blend of theoretical insights and practical applications, enabling 
students to explore the core aspects of marketing strategies, consumer behavior, market research, 
digital marketing, and the management principles that underpin successful business operations. 
 
This integrated course brings together six complementary CTS Marketing and Management 
(MAM) modules to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of modern retail, 
marketing, and service-based business operations. Students explore how organizations attract 
customers, deliver quality service, manage operations, ensure continuous improvement, and 
promote products effectively through visual and print advertising strategies. Emphasis is placed 
on practical application, employability skills, and real-world scenarios aligned with Canadian 
and Alberta business contexts. 
 
 
Course Objectives 
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: 
• Demonstrate foundational knowledge of marketing principles and management practices. 
• Apply quality customer service standards in retail and service environments. 
• Analyze and implement quality management systems to improve organizational 
performance. 
• Design and evaluate effective visual merchandising presentations. 
• Manage core retail operations, including pricing, inventory, and financial documentation. 
• Plan, design, and assess print advertising campaigns for defined target markets. 
• Evaluate the relationship between marketing, operations, service quality, and promotion 
in achieving business objectives. 
• Develop transferable workplace skills including communication, problem-solving, ethical 
decision-making, and professionalism.

MAM1010: MARKETING & MANAGEMENT 
 
Description: Students identify basic management and marketing concepts and describe retail 
merchandising strategies of value to the retail employee, manager or owner. 
 
Marketing and Management explores how organizations operate, make decisions, and connect 
products and services with consumers. Students examine management roles, business ownership 
structures, retailing in Canada, and how marketing strategies influence consumer behavior, 
profitability, and society. Emphasis is placed on real-world examples to build practical financial, 
entrepreneurial, and workplace readiness skills. 
 
Roles of Management: Refers to coordinating people and resources to achieve organizational 
goals efficiently and effectively. Key management roles include: 
Planning 
• Setting goals and determining actions to achieve them 
• Example: A retailer planning seasonal inventory 
Organizing 
• Structuring tasks, roles, and resources 
• Example: Assigning staff to departments 
Leading 
• Motivating, directing, and supporting employees 
• Example: Store manager coaching new employees 
Monitoring (Controlling) 
• Tracking performance and correcting problems 
• Example: Reviewing sales data and adjusting pricing 
Communicating 
• Sharing information clearly with employees, suppliers, and customers 
• Example: Staff meetings, emails, advertising messages 
 
Role of Retailing. Retailing is the process of selling goods and services directly to consumers 
for personal or household use. Retailers act as the link between manufacturers, wholesalers, and 
the end consumer. The role of retailing includes: 
 
1. Providing Access to Products and Services 
o Retailers make a wide variety of products available in convenient locations. 
o Example: Grocery stores, clothing stores, online marketplaces. 
2. Creating Value for Consumers 
o Retailers package, display, and market products to make shopping easier and 
more appealing. 
o Offer services like delivery, customer service, loyalty programs. 
3. Supporting the Economy 
o Retailing creates jobs (cashiers, managers, merchandisers). 
o Generates tax revenue for governments. 
o Stimulates production and innovation by creating demand. 
4. Connecting with Society 
o Retailers reflect cultural and social trends through products and marketing.

Evolution of Retailing. Retailing in Canada has Retailing in Canada has evolved from small 
local shops to complex, technology-driven omnichannel networks. Retailing is central to the 
economy, shapes consumer behavior, and continues to adapt to changing technology, culture, 
and society.  
 
Early Retail (1800s–Early 1900s) 
• General stores and small shops served local communities. 
• Products were limited, and trade was often personal (barter or small cash transactions). 
 
Department Stores & Chain Stores (1900s–1950s) 
• Large stores sold a wide variety of products under one roof. 
• Chain stores expanded across cities, offering standardized products and pricing. 
 
Suburban Retail & Shopping Malls (1960s–1980s) 
• Growth of suburbs led to shopping malls and big-box stores. 
• Increased convenience and choice for consumers. 
• Focus on customer experience and promotions. 
 
Technology & Electronic Retailing (1990s–2000s) 
• Introduction of electronic payment methods (credit/debit cards). 
• Point-of-sale scanning and inventory management improved efficiency. 
• Early e-commerce emerged. 
 
Modern Retailing & Omnichannel (2010s–Present) 
• Online retail, mobile apps, and home delivery dominate. 
• Integration of physical and digital shopping experiences (omnichannel retailing). 
• Personalized marketing and loyalty programs. 
• Focus on sustainability, cultural awareness, and ethical practices. 
 
Functions of Buying, Selling, and Merchandising. Retail businesses operate through three 
main functions that work together to meet customer needs, maximize sales, and ensure 
profitability: buying, selling, and merchandising. 
 
Buying is the process of selecting, purchasing, and managing products that a business will sell to 
consumers. 
• Products: Choosing items that meet consumer demand, trends, and quality standards. 
• Supplier: Working with suppliers to get favorable prices, delivery schedules, and terms. 
• Inventory: Maintaining appropriate stock levels to meet demand without overstocking. 
• Forecasting Trends: Predicting which products will sell well in upcoming seasons. 
• Example: A clothing store buyer decides to stock winter coats in October based on 
weather predictions, sales trends, and supplier availability. 
 
Selling is the process of interacting with customers to complete transactions and provide service. 
• Customer Assistance: Helping shoppers find the right product and answering questions.

• Transactions: Completing sales through cash, card, or online payments. 
• Relationship Building: Creating loyalty by providing a positive shopping experience. 
• Products: Highlighting features, benefits, and special offers to encourage purchases. 
• Example: A salesperson explains the features of a laptop to a customer, answers 
questions, and completes the purchase. 
 
Merchandising is the planning, presentation, and promotion of products in a way that 
encourages customers to buy. 
• Display: Arranging items to attract attention (e.g., window displays, shelf placement). 
• Packaging: Using attractive, informative packaging to influence consumer choice. 
• Pricing Strategies: Setting prices that appeal to customers while ensuring profitability. 
• Promotion: Using in-store advertising, demos, and loyalty programs to boost sales. 
• Stock Control: Ensuring products are available and replenished in the right quantities. 
• Example: A grocery store places eye-level shelves for popular cereals, uses bright 
packaging, and offers “buy one, get one free” promotions to increase sales.

Importance of Marketing. Marketing is essential to a market economy because it connects 
businesses with consumers by identifying and meeting their needs, which drives demand for 
goods and services. It encourages competition, prompting businesses to improve quality, lower 
prices, and innovate, which benefits consumers and stimulates economic growth.  
 
Marketing also helps allocate resources efficiently by guiding businesses to invest in products 
and services that are in demand, while building customer relationships and loyalty through 
promotions, branding, and engagement. In this way, marketing acts as a key driver of economic 
activity, innovation, and consumer satisfaction in a market-based system. 
 
Relationship Between Satisfying Consumers and Making a Profit. In a market economy, 
businesses exist to meet consumer needs while generating profit. These two goals are closely 
linked because satisfied customers are more likely to buy products, return for future purchases, 
and recommend business to others, all of which increase sales and revenue.

• Customer Satisfaction Drives Sales: When products or services meet or exceed 
consumer expectations, customers are more willing to spend money, leading to higher 
sales volumes. 
• Repeat Business and Loyalty: Satisfied customers are loyal customers. Loyalty reduces 
marketing costs and ensures a steady income stream. 
• Positive Reputation and Referrals: Happy consumers often share their experiences, 
attracting new customers without extra advertising costs. 
• Balancing Costs and Quality: Businesses must provide value while managing costs. 
High-quality products and services may cost more but often allow higher pricing and 
stronger brand loyalty, increasing long-term profits. 
 
Satisfying consumers is not separate from making a profit; it is a key strategy for achieving 
profitability. Businesses that prioritize consumer needs effectively build trust, loyalty, and 
revenue, creating a sustainable cycle of success. 
 
The Marketing Mix. The marketing mix is a framework businesses use to make decisions that 
meet consumer needs, compete effectively, and achieve profitability. It consists of the Four P’s 
(Product, Price, Promotion, Place) and the Two C’s (Consumers, Competition) 
 
The Four P’s 
1. Product: Refers to the goods or services a business offers to satisfy customer needs. Key 
considerations: quality, design, features, branding, packaging, and warranties. 
o Example: A smartphone with high-quality camera, sleek design, and brand 
recognition. 
2. Price: The amount customers pay for a product or service. Strategies may include 
discount pricing, premium pricing, bundle pricing, or seasonal pricing. 
o Example: A new video game might be priced higher at launch, then discounted 
later to attract more buyers. 
3. Promotion: How a business communicates with consumers to inform, persuade, or 
remind them about a product. Includes advertising, sales promotions, social media 
campaigns, sponsorships, and public relations. 
o Example: A clothing brand using Instagram ads and in-store promotions for a 
new collection. 
4. Place: The location or channels through which products are sold to consumers. Includes 
physical stores, online platforms, distributors, or direct sales. 
o Example: A bakery selling products both in-store and via online ordering system. 
 
The Two C’s 
1. Consumers: Focuses on understanding the target market: their preferences, habits, and 
needs. Helps businesses tailor products, prices, promotions, and distribution. 
o Example: A company designing age-appropriate toys based on children’s 
interests. 
2. Competition: Involves analyzing rival businesses to identify opportunities and threats. 
Helps set competitive prices, differentiate products, and design better marketing 
strategies. 
o Example: A coffee shop offering specialty drinks to stand out from nearby chains.

The marketing mix is a tool for making strategic decisions that balance consumer needs, 
competitive pressures, and business goals. By considering the Four P’s and Two C’s, businesses 
can create a strong, cohesive approach that attracts customers, increases sales, and builds long-
term success. 
 
Decision-Making. The marketing mix consists of the Four P’s (Product, Price, Promotion, 
Place) and decisions in each area directly affect a business’s success. 
 
Product decisions focus on what the business will offer and how it meets customer needs: 
• Design and Features: Choosing the look, size, quality, and functionality of a product. 
• Branding and Packaging: Selecting a brand name, logo, and packaging that appeal to the 
target market. 
• Product Variety: Deciding on product lines, models, or options. 
• After-Sales Service: Offering warranties, customer support, or maintenance. 
 
Pricing decisions determine how much customers pay and influence perceived value and sales: 
• Pricing Strategy: Choosing between premium pricing, competitive pricing, discounts, or 
bundle offers. 
• Payment Options: Allowing installment plans, credit, or loyalty program points. 
• Profit Margin: Ensuring the price covers costs and generates profit. 
 
Promotion decisions focus on how the business communicates with its target market: 
• Advertising: Selecting media channels like TV, social media, or in-store ads. 
• Sales Promotions: Offering limited-time discounts, contests, or free samples. 
• Public Relations: Managing the business’s image and reputation. 
• Personal Selling: Training staff to explain products and persuade customers effectively. 
 
Place decisions determine where and how customers access the product: 
• Distribution: Choosing between direct sales, retail stores, online platforms, wholesalers. 
• Location: Selecting store locations with high foot traffic or convenience. 
• Inventory: Ensuring products are available when and where customers want them. 
 
By carefully analyzing each component, businesses can satisfy consumer needs, compete 
effectively, and achieve profit. Every decision in the marketing mix is interconnected: 
• Product decisions define what is sold, 
• Price decisions influence how consumers perceive value, 
• Promotion decisions determine how customers learn about the product, and 
• Place decisions ensure the product is accessible. 
 
Marketing Focus by Business Type. Marketing strategies vary depending on the role a business 
plays in the supply chain. Each type of business, manufacturers, wholesalers, and retailers, has a 
unique focus when marketing its products or services. 
 
Manufacturers: Businesses that produce goods from raw materials or components. Focus: 
• Focus on product and service development to meet consumer needs.

• Emphasize quality, features, and innovation to attract intermediaries (wholesalers and 
retailers) who will sell their products. 
• Target market is often businesses (B2B) rather than end consumers. 
• Example: A Canadian electronics manufacturer markets its high-resolution TVs to major 
retail chains rather than directly to households. 
 
Wholesalers: Businesses that buy products in bulk from manufacturers and sell them to retailers 
or other businesses. Focus: 
• Promote products and services to retailers rather than end consumers. 
• Emphasize competitive pricing, reliable supply, and product variety. 
• Relationship-building with retailers to ensure long-term contracts and consistent orders. 
• Example: A beverage wholesaler markets soda and juice products to grocery stores and 
convenience stores across Alberta, highlighting volume discounts and timely delivery. 
 
Retailers: Businesses that sell products directly to the end consumer for personal use. Focus: 
• Focus on meeting consumer needs and preferences. 
• Emphasize customer experience, convenience, promotions, and loyalty programs. 
• Use merchandising, advertising, and pricing strategies to attract and retain consumers. 
• Example: A clothing store markets seasonal collections to local shoppers through social 
media, in-store displays, and discounts. 
 
The focus of marketing shifts along the supply chain: manufacturers market to businesses, 
wholesalers market to retailers, and retailers market directly to consumers. Each stage requires 
strategies suited to its target audience and role in delivering products. 
 
Marketing Decisions on Society. Marketing decisions do more than influence consumer 
purchases, they impact society, culture, and the environment. Businesses must consider these 
effects to operate ethically and sustainably. Responsible marketing considers not only profit but 
also the long-term effects on society and the environment. 
 
• Environmental Impact: Marketing decisions about packaging, product materials, and 
production methods can affect natural resources and waste. Example: Excessive plastic 
packaging contributes to pollution, while eco-friendly packaging reduces impact. 
• Cultural and Social Influence: Advertising and product promotion shape social norms, 
trends, and consumer behavior. Example: Fashion or tech marketing may influence 
lifestyle choices or spending habits. 
• Ethical Considerations: Misleading advertising, false claims, or targeting vulnerable 
populations can harm consumers and society. Example: Promoting unhealthy food to 
children can have long-term health effects. 
• Economic Effects: Marketing drives demand, which affects job creation, economic 
growth, and resource allocation. Example: Successful marketing campaigns for a new 
product line can create manufacturing and retail jobs. 
• Community and Social Responsibility: Businesses can use marketing to promote positive 
societal change, such as sustainability, diversity, or charitable initiatives. Example: 
Campaigns encouraging recycling or donating a portion of sales to community programs.

Marketing and retail merchandising are related but distinct business functions. Marketing is a 
broad, strategic process focused on understanding consumer needs, creating demand, and 
promoting products or services to target markets. It involves decisions about the product, price, 
promotion, place, consumers, and competition to achieve business goals and profitability.  
 
Retail merchandising, on the other hand, is more tactical and focuses on the presentation and 
promotion of products within the store or sales environment to encourage purchases. This 
includes product placement, packaging, pricing strategies, displays, and in-store promotions. In 
essence, marketing sets the strategy to attract and satisfy customers, while retail merchandising 
executes these strategies at the point of sale to maximize sales and enhance the experience. 
 
Role of Technology in Retail Evolution. Technology has dramatically transformed retailing in 
Canada and worldwide by improving efficiency, convenience, and customer experience. 
Retailers use technological innovations to streamline operations, enhance product quality, and 
meet consumer expectations. 
 
• Electronic Banking (Debit and Credit Cards): Replaced cash as the primary payment 
method, making transactions faster, more secure, and convenient for consumers. 
Example: Shoppers can pay instantly using debit or credit cards, which also allows 
retailers to track sales data and customer spending patterns. 
• Home Shopping (Online Retailing): Enabled consumers to browse and purchase 
products from home, expanding market reach beyond physical store locations. Example: 
E-commerce platforms like Amazon or Canadian online grocery services allow customers 
to shop 24/7 and have products delivered to their door. 
• Scanners and Universal Product Codes (UPCs): Automated the checkout process, 
improved inventory management, and reduced errors in pricing. Example: UPC barcodes 
allow cashiers to scan items quickly, track stock levels, and reorder products efficiently. 
• Improved Product Quality: Technology in manufacturing and production has raised 
product standards, consistency, and reliability. Example: Advanced machinery in 
electronics or food production ensures higher-quality goods, reducing defects and 
increasing customer satisfaction. 
• Just-in-Time (JIT) Delivery: Optimizes inventory levels by delivering products only 
when needed, reducing storage costs and waste. Example: Retailers like grocery stores 
receive daily shipments of fresh produce based on predicted consumer demand, ensuring 
freshness and availability. 
 
Technology has revolutionized retailing by enhancing convenience, efficiency, and quality. 
Electronic payments simplify transactions, online shopping expands market access, scanners and 
UPCs improve inventory management, production technology raises product standards, and just-
in-time delivery reduces costs while meeting consumer needs. Together, these innovations allow 
retailers to respond faster, serve customers better, and compete in the modern marketplace. 
 
Product Merchandising Strategies to Increase Sales. Product merchandising involves 
planning, presenting, and promoting products in ways that encourage consumers to buy. 
Retailers use several strategies to increase visibility, appeal, and sales.

• Scrambled Merchandising: Offering a wide variety of unrelated products in the same 
store to attract more customers. Example: A convenience store selling snacks, household 
items, electronics, and lottery tickets to meet different consumer needs in one trip. 
 
• Narrowing the Product Line: Focusing on a smaller, specialized range of products to 
better meet customer preferences and reduce inventory complexity. Example: A boutique 
clothing store specializing only in women’s formal wear, attracting a targeted customer 
base seeking specific products. 
 
• Sampling and Product Demonstrations: Allowing customers to try products before 
purchasing or showing how products work. Example: A grocery store offering free 
samples of a new yogurt brand or a tech store demonstrating a new smartphone model. 
 
• Shelf Positioning (Eye-Level Placement): Placing products at eye level to maximize 
visibility and encourage impulse purchases. Example: Popular cereal brands positioned at 
eye level in supermarkets to increase the likelihood of selection. 
 
• Packaging: Designing attractive, informative packaging that draws attention and 
communicates the product’s value. Example: Brightly colored snack packaging with clear 
labels and appealing images to entice consumers. 
 
• Brand Selection and Identification: Highlighting well-known brands or creating strong 
brand identity to influence consumer choice. Example: A grocery store promoting Coca-
Cola products with recognizable logos and branded displays. 
 
Effective product merchandising strategies increase sales by making products more visible, 
attractive, and accessible to consumers. Retailers combine techniques such as scrambled 
merchandising, specialized product lines, sampling, strategic shelf placement, appealing 
packaging, and strong brand promotion to maximize customer interest and encourage purchases. 
 
Pricing Merchandising Strategies to Increase Sales. Pricing merchandising strategies are used 
by retailers to influence consumer buying behavior, encourage purchases, and maximize 
profitability. These strategies help attract customers and create perceived value for products. 
1. Multiple Pricing: Offering several items together at a single price, often lower than 
buying each individually. Example: “3 for $10” deals on canned beverages or snacks 
encourage customers to buy more than they originally planned. 
2. Unit Pricing on Shelves: Displaying the price per unit (e.g., per kilogram, per litre) to 
help consumers compare products and see value. Example: Supermarkets label cereal 
boxes with price per 100g so shoppers can easily compare brands. 
3. Warehouse Pricing: Selling products in bulk at a lower price per unit to encourage large 
purchases. Example: Wholesale clubs like Costco offer large packs of paper towels or 
juice at a lower per-item cost than regular stores. 
4. Loss Leaders: Pricing a popular product below cost to attract customers, hoping they 
will buy additional higher-margin items. Example: A grocery store sells milk at a very 
low price to bring customers in, knowing they will also purchase other full-priced items.

Pricing strategies are tools for influencing consumer behavior, increasing sales volume, and 
encouraging purchases. Techniques like multiple pricing, unit pricing, warehouse pricing, and 
loss leaders help retailers attract customers, provide value, and boost overall profitability. 
 
Service Merchandising Strategies to Increase Sales. Service merchandising focuses on 
enhancing the customer experience and offering additional services to encourage purchases, 
build loyalty, and differentiate a business from competitors. 
1. Hours of Operation: Extending store hours to provide convenience for customers. 
Example: A grocery store staying open late on weekends attracts shoppers who cannot 
visit during regular hours. 
2. Franchising (Consistency and Reliability): Offering standardized products and services 
across multiple locations to build trust and brand loyalty. Example: Tim Hortons ensures 
that coffee, donuts, and service quality are consistent in every Canadian location. 
3. Loyalty Programs: Rewarding repeat customers to encourage continued purchases. 
Example: A coffee shop offers a points system where every 10 coffees purchased earn a 
free drink. 
4. Delivery, Gift Wrapping, Installation, or Repair: Providing additional services that 
make shopping easier or add value for the customer. Example: Furniture stores offering 
home delivery and assembly, or electronics stores providing installation services. 
5. Satisfaction Guaranteed: Offering refunds, exchanges, or warranties to give customers 
confidence in their purchase. Example: A retailer allows customers to return clothing 
within 30 days with no questions asked, encouraging more purchases. 
 
Service strategies increase sales by enhancing convenience, building trust, and creating positive 
customer experience. By providing extended hours, loyalty programs, additional services, and 
satisfaction guarantee, businesses attract more customers, encourage repeat business, and 
strengthen brand reputation. 
 
Place Merchandising Strategies to Increase Sales. Place merchandising focuses on how and 
where products are made available to consumers. Effective placement strategies enhance 
convenience, visibility, and overall shopping experience, which can increase sales. 
1. Size of the Store: Ensuring the store is appropriately sized to display products 
attractively and accommodate customer traffic. Example: Large supermarkets allow for 
wide aisles and ample displays, making shopping easier and encouraging purchases. 
2. Layout of the Store: Strategically arranging products to guide customer flow, highlight 
key items, and encourage impulse buys. Example: Placing commonly purchased items, 
like milk or bread, around the store perimeter so shoppers pass other products. 
3. Use of Direct Lighting: Using lighting to highlight products, attract attention, and 
enhance their appearance. Example: Jewelry stores use spotlights on display cases to 
make rings and watches sparkle and catch customers’ eyes. 
 
Merchandising strategies help businesses optimize the physical environment to improve product 
visibility, convenience, and customer experience. By focusing on store size, layout, and lighting, 
retailers encourage longer shopping visits, impulse purchases, and ultimately, higher sales.

Promotional Strategies to Increase Sales. Promotional merchandising focuses on attracting 
attention, informing customers, and encouraging purchases through various marketing tools and 
displays. Effective promotions can increase awareness, drive traffic, and boost sales. 
1. Visual Merchandising: Using attractive displays and arrangements to showcase 
products and capture customer interest. Example: Window displays featuring seasonal 
products or themed layouts that draw shoppers into the store. 
2. In-Store Posters and Advertising: Placing posters or signs around the store that 
coordinate with broader promotional campaigns. Example: A poster near the entrance

3. Shelf Cards Indicating Specials: Using small signs or tags on shelves to highlight

One Free” on a popular snack encourages immediate purchase. 
4. Packaging and Labelling: Designing packaging to attract attention, convey information, 
or reinforce promotions. Example: Brightly colored packaging with “Limited Edition” 
labels or promotional messages to entice buyers. 
 
Promotional merchandising strategies increase product visibility, attract customer attention, and 
stimulate purchases. Techniques like visual displays, in-store posters, shelf cards, and eye-
catching packaging help retailers communicate value, create excitement, and drive sales.

MAM1020: QUALITY CUSTOMER SERVICE 
 
Description: Students identify and describe the target customer and the selling floor, including 
sales and nonsales activities. They will demonstrate techniques required by employees in the 
field. Quality customer service is a critical skill in every industry. Whether working in retail, 
hospitality, healthcare, trades, or business ownership, understanding customers and delivering 
consistent, respectful service is essential for success. 
 
What Is a Target Market? A target market is a specific group of consumers that a business 
aims to sell its products or services to. Businesses focus on target markets to better meet 
customer needs and increase success. 
 
Participants in a Target Market. A target market is not just a group of people, it is made up of 
specific participants who play different roles in the buying and usage process. Understanding 
each participant helps businesses tailor products, services, and marketing strategies effectively. 
 
Buyers: Buyers are the people who actually make the purchase of a product or service. They 
control the money and the decision to buy. Their priorities often include price, quality, 
convenience, and perceived value. Buyers may not always be the end-users. 
Example: A parent buying shoes for their child is the buyer, even though the child will wear the 
shoes. A company purchasing office supplies is the buyer, while employees are the users. 
 
Users: Users are the people who use or consume the product or service. Users may or may not 
influence the purchase. Understanding user needs is essential for product design, functionality, 
and satisfaction. User experience drives repeat purchases and brand loyalty. 
Example: In the shoes example, the child is the user. A student using educational software 
purchased by the school is the user. 
 
Influencers: Influencers are individuals or groups who affect the buying decision, but may not 
purchase or use the product themselves. They can be family members, friends, colleagues,

employees to suggest improvements, and builds a culture of shared responsibility.

audits and reviews, focus on meeting customer and regulatory requirements, ensures consistency 
in products or services, reduces mistakes, builds customer trust and credibility.

involvement in problem-solving

Product and Fashion Life Cycle. The product and fashion life cycle describes the stages a 
product goes through from introduction to removal from the market. Both typically include four 
stages: introduction, growth, maturity, and decline. Fashion items usually move through this 
cycle much faster than basic products, as styles and trends change quickly, making timing and 
inventory management especially important for retailers. 
 
Stages: 
1. Introduction: In this stage, sales are low as the product is launched and awareness is built. 
2. Growth: Demand increases, sales rise, and profits improve as the product gains 
acceptance. 
3. Maturity: Is marked by peak sales, increased competition, and stable but slower growth, 
often requiring promotions to maintain market share. 
4. Decline: Sales decrease due to changing consumer preferences, new products, or trends.

buyers forecast demand and determine appropriate quantities.

manufacturers, wholesalers, trade shows, sales representatives, catalogues, and online vendor 
platforms. Buyers also consider supplier reputation, product quality, pricing, availability, and 
delivery reliability when evaluating sources. Together, buying data and sources allows buyers to 
select the right products at the right price and time to meet customer needs while controlling 
costs and inventory.

clearly. A requisition form is used internally to request approval to purchase goods, confirming 
that the items are needed and within budget.

document that specifies the items ordered, quantities, prices, delivery terms, and payment 
conditions. Together, these forms help prevent ordering errors, control spending, provide a 
record for receiving and invoicing, and support accurate recordkeeping and accountability.

the goods are still usable. 
➢ Overage or shortage, the buyer compares the shipment to the purchase order and 
packing slip, then reports any discrepancies to the supplier. The buyer may return excess 
items, request missing items, or have the invoice adjusted to reflect the actual quantity 
received. 
➢ Lost or misplaced, the buyer can track the shipment using shipping documentation, 
contact the supplier or carrier, and file a claim if necessary. The buyer may request a 
replacement shipment or a refund, depending on the shipping terms and responsibility for

Pricing, Markups, and Markdown. Markup is the difference between the cost of a product and 
its selling (retail) price, expressed either as a dollar amount or as a percentage. It represents the 
amount added to the cost to cover expenses and generate a profit. When calculated based on cost, 
the formula is: 
Markup (%) = Retail Price – Cost Price

This shows how much above the cost the item is sold for. For example, if an item costs $50 and 
is sold for $75, the markup is $25, or 50% of the cost. Retailers use markup to set prices that

another method, which expresses the profit as a percentage of the final selling price, but the cost-
based method is the most commonly used in retail operations. 
 
Break Evan Point. Is the level of sales at which a business covers all its costs, meaning total 
revenue equals total expenses, and there is neither profit nor loss. It helps retailers determine 
how much they need to sell to avoid losing money. 
 
Formula: 
Break-even Point (units) = Fixed Costs
Selling Price per Unit – Variable Cost per Unit 
 
• Fixed Costs: Costs that do not change with sales volume (e.g., rent, salaries). 
• Variable Costs: Costs that change with production or sales (e.g., cost of goods sold). 
• Selling Price per Unit: The retail price of each item. 
 
Example: 
• Fixed Costs = $2,000 
• Variable Cost per Unit = $20 
• Selling Price per Unit = $50 
Break-even Point = 2,000
50 − 20 = 2,000
30 ≈ 67 units 
 
The retailer must sell approximately 67 units to cover all costs. Selling more units generates 
profit; selling fewer results in a loss. The break-even point is a critical tool for pricing, inventory, 
and sales planning in retail operations.

Pricing policies are strategies retailers use to set the selling price of goods in a way that achieves 
business objectives, attracts customers, and remains competitive. Different policies have distinct 
applications and effects: 
 
➢ Market Penetration Pricing: Setting a low initial price to attract customers and gain 
market share quickly. Effect: Encourages high sales volume and customer loyalty but 
may result in lower short-term profit. 
➢ Price Skimming: Setting a high initial price for new or unique products to maximize 
profit from early adopters. Effect: Generates high profit per unit but may limit the number 
of buyers initially. 
➢ Comparable or Competitive Pricing: Pricing products in line with competitors’ prices 
for similar items. Effect: Helps remain competitive, avoids price wars, and maintains 
perceived fairness in the market. 
➢ Flexible Pricing: Using variable pricing strategies such as one-price (fixed) or negotiable 
pricing. Effect: Allows adaptation to different customers or market conditions but 
requires careful management to avoid confusion or perceived unfairness. 
➢ Relative Pricing: Setting prices based on the desired image, perceived value, or target 
profit margin. Effect: Positions products according to brand strategy, influencing 
customer perception and purchase decisions.

turnover. Retailers select and apply policies based on product type, market demand, competition,

Inventory Control. Retailers use different methods of inventory control to track stock, prevent 
shortages or overstocking, and manage costs effectively. Each method helps retailers balance 
inventory availability, reduce costs, and improve efficiency. Common methods include: 
 
➢ Periodic Inventory: Inventory is counted at regular intervals (e.g., weekly, monthly, or 
annually) to determine stock levels and calculate cost of goods sold. Suitable for small 
businesses with limited inventory. 
➢ Perpetual Inventory: Inventory records are continuously updated as items are received, 
sold, or returned, often using computer systems or barcode scanning. This provides real-
time stock levels and accurate financial data. 
➢ Just-in-Time (JIT) Inventory: Stock is ordered and received only as needed to meet 
demand, minimizing storage costs and reducing excess inventory. This method requires 
reliable suppliers and careful demand forecasting. 
➢ ABC Analysis: Inventory is categorized by value and importance (A = high-value, B = 
moderate-value, C = low-value), allowing retailers to focus control efforts on the most 
critical items. 
➢ Minimum-Maximum Stock Levels: Establishes a minimum and maximum quantity for 
each item to maintain adequate supply while avoiding overstocking.

Introduction to Advertising. Advertising is a paid, non-personal form of communication used 
by businesses, organizations, or individuals to promote products, services, ideas, or causes to a 
specific audience. Its main purpose is to inform consumers about products or services, persuade

Publicity and advertising are both tools used to communicate messages about products,

while publicity is unpaid and often controlled by external media. 
• Cost: Advertising is paid for by the organization, whereas publicity is usually free and 
generated by media coverage or public interest. 
• Control: In advertising, the company has full control over the message, design, and 
timing. In publicity, the organization has limited control because the media decides how 
the story is presented. 
• Purpose: Advertising aims to promote and sell products or services, while publicity often 
seeks to inform, create awareness, or generate interest without direct payment.

stereotypes. 
4. Materialism and Overconsumption: Encourages excessive spending or unrealistic 
lifestyles.

Advantages: 
• Tangible and can be kept for reference. 
• Targeted distribution (local, regional, or niche audiences). 
• Allows for detailed information and visuals. 
• Can be cost-effective for small audiences or local campaigns. 
Disadvantages: 
• Declining readership due to digital media. 
• Limited interactivity with the audience. 
• Production and placement costs can be high for larger campaigns. 
• Ads may be overlooked or ignored (especially in newspapers). 
 
Broadcast Media: refers to audio-visual channels that transmit advertising messages to a large 
audience. Examples: Television, Radio 
 
Advantages: 
• Wide reach; can target millions of viewers or listeners. 
• Engaging through sight, sound, and motion (TV) or voice (radio). 
• Creates strong brand recognition and emotional appeal. 
• Ideal for mass-market products or time-sensitive promotions.

Components of a print advertisement. A well-designed print advertisement combines borders, 
headline(s), illustrations/graphics, copy, and a logo to capture attention, communicate the 
message clearly, and create brand recognition. Each component plays a specific role in guiding 
the reader’s attention and persuading them to act. 
 
• Borders: The frame or outline around the ad that separates it from surrounding content. 
Helps focus attention on the advertisement and gives it structure. Example: A thick 
border around a flyer making it stand out on a bulletin board. 
 
• Headline(s): The main text or phrase that captures the reader’s attention. Grabs attention 
immediately and conveys the key message. Example: “Summer Sale – Up to 50% Off!” 
 
• Illustrations or Graphics: Images, photographs, or drawings included in the ad. Attracts 
attention, supports the message, and helps the audience visualize the product. Example: A 
picture of a new smartphone showing its design and features. 
 
• Copy: The written text that explains details about the product, service, or offer. Provides 
information, explains benefits, and persuades the reader to take action. Example: “Our 
new organic coffee is fair-trade certified and roasted locally for the freshest taste.” 
 
• Logo (Signature): The company’s symbol, trademark, or name used consistently across 
all ads. Ensures brand recognition and builds trust with the audience. Example: The 
McDonald’s golden arches at the bottom of a flyer. 
 
Costs of Advertisements vs. Return on Investment (ROI). When planning advertisements, 
businesses must consider both the cost of creating and placing an ad and the return on investment 
(ROI) the financial or strategic benefit gained from the campaign. 
 
Advertisement Costs 
• Creation Costs: Expenses for designing the ad, including graphics, photography, 
copywriting, and layout. 
• Placement Costs: Fees for publishing the ad in a chosen medium: 
o Print (newspapers, magazines, flyers) 
o Broadcast (TV, radio) 
o Digital (social media, websites) 
• Example: A full-page magazine ad may cost several thousand dollars, whereas a local 
flyer may cost only a few hundred. 
 
Measuring Return on Investment (ROI). ROI measures how much benefit the advertisement 
generates compared to its cost.

• Formula: 
ROI (%) = Gain from Advertisement – Cost of Advertisement

• Example: 
o Cost of ad: $2,000 
o Sales generated: $5,000

Comparison Considerations: 
• High-Cost Ads: TV commercials or full-page national magazine ads may reach large 
audiences but are expensive. The ROI must justify the cost. 
• Low-Cost Ads: Flyers, local posters, or social media ads are cheaper but may have a 
smaller reach. ROI may be high if the target market is effectively reached. 
• Targeted Approach: Ads that are highly targeted often generate better ROI because they 
reach the audience most likely to respond. 
 
When planning advertisements, businesses must balance costs with expected returns. A 
successful ad campaign maximizes ROI by ensuring that the benefits, sales, awareness, or brand 
recognition, exceed the expenses of creating and placing the ad. 
 
Steps in Planning a Print Advertisement 
 
1.  Determine the Form of Print Media: Decide the type of print medium that best suits 
your message and target audience. Considerations: Audience reach, cost, and placement 
location. Examples: Flyer, poster, brochure, magazine ad, newspaper ad, or billboard. 
2. State the Objective: Clearly define the purpose of the advertisement. Examples: 
Increase sales of a product, Promote a service, Build brand awareness, Announce an 
event or promotion 
3. Define the Target Audience: Identify the group of people most likely to respond 
positively to the ad. Factors to consider: Age, gender, income, lifestyle, location, 
interests. Example: Teenagers for a new video game release, adults 25–40 for a fitness 
program. 
4. Select the Buying Motive / Unique Selling Proposition (USP): Determine what will 
persuade the audience to take action. USP: The feature or benefit that makes the 
product/service unique. Example: “Our coffee is 100% organic and locally roasted” or 
“Save 30% this weekend only.” 
5. Plan the Layout and Components: Decide on the design and placement of ad elements: 
borders, headline, graphics, copy, and logo. Consider effective use of white space, font 
styles, and visual hierarchy to attract attention and convey the message clearly. 
 
Planning a print advertisement involves a step-by-step process: choosing the medium, setting 
clear objectives, defining the audience, identifying what will motivate them to act, and designing 
the layout effectively. A well-planned ad ensures that the message reaches the right audience in a 
clear and persuasive way.
